captions.instagram:
Moved to the US mid-year on an H-1B? Your first tax year may be dual-status: nonresident before your residency start date, resident after.

✔️ Arrived July 1 and stayed? That's 184 days by Dec. 31, enough for the 183-day test.
✔️ Resident on Dec. 31: Form 1040 with "Dual-Status Return" on top, plus a statement for the nonresident part.
✔️ In a dual-status year you can't take the standard deduction or file as head of household.
✔️ A joint return is possible only by choosing to be treated as residents for the whole year, which means reporting worldwide income.

We prepare H-1B returns, federal plus NJ and NY (our standard 1040 pricing). Book a call to check your first year. Not available for CA, CT, MD or OR state returns.

Tax information only, not immigration advice.

sources.fact: Dual-status years are most common in years of arrival/departure; resident on last day: file Form 1040 marked "Dual-Status Return" with a statement for the nonresident part; no standard deduction; no joint return unless married to a citizen/resident and electing; no head of household (page updated 23-Nov-2025, read 2026-10-25)
Residency starting date under the substantial presence test is generally the first day present in the US that year (read 2026-10-25)
Choice to treat a nonresident spouse as resident: both report worldwide income; signed statement attached to the joint return (read 2026-10-25)
H-1B who meets the substantial presence test is a US resident for federal income tax; dual-status aliens file a special return (read 2026-10-24)
July 1 to Dec. 31 = 184 days (31+31+30+31+30+31), which meets 183 with no prior-year days
